rv.q: I found it brilliantly, bizarrely funny, the sort of auteur performance that no other actor alive would so much as think of giving.
Smith-Cameron really is the heart and soul of this production, for all of Rylance’s charisma.
Rylance’s charisma knits together a production that’s full of roustabout hilarity and poignancy mingled together, bright and bleak at once.

Smith-Cameron is splendid in her calm constancy, bringing a liberal helping of Gerri’s steely watchfulness to Juno as she navigates to the limits of a patriarchal society further hemmed in by the all-controlling Catholic Church.
In this enjoyable Gielgud staging, director Matthew Warchus, in particular, still doesn’t seem to know quite what to make of Johnny Boyle, or how to handle his subplot.
But though the play has historic value and potent moments it feels hopelessly over the top in this staging.
But his performance is also so overdone and insistent that it unbalances the play, drawing focus from other characters and undermining the darker elements.
While there are some hilarious set pieces and some compelling moments of pathos, the production never recovers from its uneven energy and slack pace.
Yet, Rylance, boozy brilliance notwithstanding, serves up a risky, highly mannered performance, full of actorly tics and affectations.
He is tapping into the slurred vaudevillian razzmatazz he gave us in Jerusalem, but in his own silo.
Warchus and Rylance haven’t pulled off the same trick here.
Although the change was agreed with the O’Casey estate, it still strikes me as failing to understand the pain of this great and tragic comedy.

It is easy to see from Matthew Warchus’s compelling revival of Sean O’Casey’s tragi-comic play Juno and the Paycock, about the cost of poverty and war on humanity, why it is called ‘The Irish Masterpiece.’
Matthew Warchus’s production negotiates the changes of mood to excellent effect.
This staging still makes O’Casey’s grimly resonant point about the futile horror of civil war and sectarian politics.
This is an unusual revival, giving both the comedy and tragedy full scope.
Poetic and poignant, this potentially great revival feels a little too uneven to soar.
The best parts of the play don’t feature the best actor.
Despite the faithful attention to O’Casey’s lines, this version of Juno and the Paycock is more a vehicle for the comedy talents of Rylance, and it’s sure to please the legions of his fans.
A tepid and sluggish show that took a long, long time to make the point that life is s**t and then you die.
It’s a deep disappointment on every level, a reminder that star dust can sometimes cloud the picture rather than illuminate it.
It is both brilliant and painful to watch.
